title: Guru Ram Das: devotion
hookLine: the fourth Guru's light: the pool of nectar and the four rounds
tomorrow: how can anyone call a hard will sweet?

cards: Sleep apps sell rain on a loop, and a creek, and an ocean you can't see. Baba Kartar prefers the real thing. Every morning now he walks to the little pond at the park, sits on the same bench, and closes his eyes.
Simran walks with him today and asks: why water? He says the fourth Guru began a pool, and a city grew up around it. The city still carries the pool's name: Amritsar, the pool of nectar.

teach.b: Today's question: what does devotion look like on an ordinary morning? Guru Ram Das answers with a routine, in Gauri ki Var, Ang 305.

In paraphrase: whoever calls themself a Sikh of the true Guru rises early, makes the effort, bathes in the pool of nectar, and meditates on the Name. Devotion here isn't a feeling that visits once. It's a morning, kept.

The same Guru wrote the Lavan, on Ang 773 and 774: the four rounds a Sikh couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib at their wedding, each round a deeper step of love toward God. Devotion has stages, and you keep walking.
Now a neighbor who pictures it with water too.
A psalm sung by Jews and Christians says, in the King James words: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God." A deer, thirsty, running toward water.
What's shared: love for God pictured as water, something you can't live without. The honest difference: the psalm's voice is still on the way, thirsty.
Guru Ram Das's Sikh is already in the pool each morning, and the nectar is the Name. Two pictures, thirst and a daily dip, and each tradition keeps its own.
One to tell a friend tonight: tradition says the pool at Amritsar came first, and the Golden Temple was built in the middle of it.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Ram Das as the Guru who began the sarovar at Amritsar; at a Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib as his four Lavan are read and sung.

o: the Guru who first wrote down the words of the Ardas
a bard whose hymns praise the Gurus in the Granth
the fourth Guru: devotion as a pool and a daily morning

games.q: the fourth Guru — tap the pairs.
p: rise early, bathe, remember the Name
the four rounds of a Sikh wedding
as the hart panteth after the water

s: in Guru Ram Das's verse, devotion is a feeling that comes and goes
it's a routine: rise early, make the effort, bathe, remember the Name.
Guru Ram Das wrote the Lavan, the four wedding rounds
Raag Suhi, Ang 773-774: four rounds, each a step of love.
the psalm and Guru Ram Das say exactly the same thing
both picture love for God as water; one is thirst on the way, one a daily dip.

games.q: your aunt says she's 'not devoted' because she never feels a big spiritual high, though she reads her prayers every dawn. what fits Guru Ram Das?
o: she's devoted; for him devotion is a morning kept, not a feeling.
she's right; devotion is the high, and the routine is just habit.
she needs a new practice that will bring the feeling back.
games.why: Ang 305 describes devotion as a routine: rise, make the effort, bathe, remember the Name. the morning kept is the devotion.

practice: If you can, sit near water: a tap barely running, a glass you fill slowly, rain, a fountain. Listen only to that sound for the whole sit.
When your mind wanders, let the water bring it back, the way each morning brings Baba Kartar back to his bench.

wordCard.voice: Guru Ram Das: the fourth Guru, whose light is devotion. He gave the Sikhs a pool, a morning routine of the Name, and the four rounds.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: laavan, the four rounds of the Sikh wedding hymn, written by Guru Ram Das.

carryVoice: Keep this: devotion, a morning kept and a pool returned to. Baba Kartar is still on his bench.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 305 (Gauri ki Var, Mahalla 4: 'gur satgur kaa jo sikh akhaae...': rise early, make the effort, bathe in the pool of nectar, meditate on the Name), paraphrased
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 773-774 (Raag Suhi, Mahalla 4, the Lavan: four rounds), paraphrased

sources.q: As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition: the sarovar at Amritsar begun under Guru Ram Das; the Harmandir Sahib built in it under Guru Arjan
